For me, this is a lesson for all of us in marketing.

Engagement reports should sit alongside questions about trust, customer retention and reputation. A post can perform well on the dashboard while damaging the business behind it.

Before we ask, “How many people will talk about this?” we need to ask, “Will our customers still feel respected after they see it?”

What concerns me is how easily a brand controversy can turn into people attacking each other’s nationality.

A brand should be held accountable for its actions. But that shouldn’t become a reason to judge an entire country.

The question is: could this issue spill beyond the brand and affect how Malaysians and Indonesians see—and treat—each other?

If I were managing the crisis, my priorities would be:

Pause promotional content. Align everyone handling responses. Acknowledge the specific mistake. Explain the corrective action.

I would also track cancellations, sales and retailer feedback.

Viral criticism signals a risk. Actual business data tells us how far that risk has translated into damage.

An apology needs to answer more than “Are they sorry?”

Customers should be able to understand:
What went wrong?
Does the brand understand why it hurt?
What will prevent it from happening again?

Blaming the admin would leave the bigger question unanswered: how did the company’s publishing process allow it?

The business has to own what its official account publishes.

The consequences can reach beyond the comment section.

Retailers may have to answer uncomfortable questions. Customer service teams absorb the anger. Creators and distributors may find their own reputations pulled into the issue. One team publishes the post, but many people can end up carrying the cost.

That is why content approval is a business responsibility.

This is where marketing judgment matters.

Before posting, we often ask: “Will this get engagement?”

But we should also ask: “Who could feel disrespected by this, and what could it cost the brand?”

An official account speaks for the business. Customers, retailers and partners can all feel the consequences of one post.

That’s why cultural awareness and a proper approval process are part of marketing.

A brand can celebrate their country’s achievements without making customers from another country feel small.

Once you sell across borders, your responsibility grows with your market.

Your content might be intended for a local audience, but screenshots travel. Context gets lost. And customers elsewhere will judge what they see.
